g.text: Three of the four stores are not databases - and the relational one holds the smallest dataset
The 60 PB dataset needs the least machinery (dumb blobs plus a CDN); the 100 GB dataset needs the most sophisticated engine (fuzzy multilingual text).

routing tiles

is it a database?
no
no
sort of
no
The mismatch on every row is why one store would be wrong.
Map tiles: an index plus a deduplicated blob store - one indirection, three payoffs
# the index: which content does this tile coordinate point at?
tile_index: (version, z, x, y) -> content_hash
# the store: one object per DISTINCT tile content
blobs: content_hash -> bytes (Mapbox Vector Tile)
storage collapses by orders of magnitude
the nominal 60 PB is a ceiling, not an estimate.
a new map version costs only what CHANGED
v42 shares every unchanged content_hash with v41, so publishing a version is a
small delta rather than a 60 PB copy - which is what makes versioning-over-purging
affordable in the first place.
the CDN caches better
one hot ocean tile is a single cached object at each edge, instead of billions of
distinct COLD objects - directly attacking the cold-tile problem.
Why object storage and not a database: the access pattern is 'fetch this
immutable blob by key', the objects are large-ish, and they are never queried by
attribute. A database would layer query planning, transactions and indexing over
what is fundamentally a file read - and no relational or document store is
designed for trillions of rows of opaque bytes.
In practice tile_index is not even a live lookup on the read path: the CDN URL encodes (version, z, x, y) directly and the
origin resolves it - so the index is consulted only on the ~1% of requests that miss the edge.
Routing tiles: graph data, and deliberately NOT a graph database
routing_tile: (version, geohash, detail_level) -> bytes
# inside the blob, a compact binary encoding:
# nodes[]: intersection id, lat, lng
# edges[]: from_node, to_node, length_m, road_class, speed_limit,
# turn_restrictions, segment_id <- the join key to traffic
# boundary[]: neighbouring tile refs + the nodes where roads cross out
Because there is no graph QUERY to run. The navigation service does not ask 'find
me a path' of the store - it asks 'give me tile 9q8yy at level 3' and runs its
own A* in memory. A graph database's value is SERVER-SIDE TRAVERSAL, and here
traversal must happen in the application because it needs custom heuristics,
level transitions and per-request user filters. You would be paying for a
traversal engine you cannot use.
And the blob is a compact BINARY format, not JSON: edges are fixed-width records
so the in-memory representation is close to the on-disk one - no parse step, and
adjacency can be an array index rather than a pointer chase. That matters because
the search is bounded by MEMORY LATENCY rather than by graph size, and
cache-friendly layout is the direct lever on it.
segment_id is the join key that makes the ETA separation work: the tile carries STATIC properties only, and live
travel time is looked up by segment_id from the traffic store. That is what lets weights change every few seconds
while tiles stay immutable - a separation of change rates, expressed as a foreign key.
Live traffic: 1.6 GB in memory, and the TTL is doing real work
KEY speed:{segment_id}
VALUE (current_speed_mps: f32, sample_count: u16, updated_at: u32)
TTL 900 seconds
100M segments x ~16 bytes is about 1.6 GB - read on every route computation,
written continuously by the traffic aggregator. The TTL does the same triple duty
as in nearby friends: it bounds memory, bounds staleness, and - most usefully -
makes 'no recent data for this segment' an AUTOMATIC state rather than something
to detect. When a key expires, the ETA service falls back to historical or
speed-limit estimates with no explicit 'is this stale?' check anywhere.
sample_count is carried because a speed derived from 3 vehicles deserves less confidence than one from 300, and the ETA model
weights it accordingly. Storing the aggregate without its sample size would throw away the information needed to know whether
to trust it.
2.4 TB/day of raw traces exist to produce a 2 TB table that never grows
CREATE TABLE location_history (
user_id bigint,
bucket int, -- DAY NUMBER: bounds partition size
ts timestamp,
lat float,
lng float,
accuracy_m smallint,
speed_mps float,
heading_deg smallint,
PRIMARY KEY ((user_id, bucket), ts)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (ts DESC)
AND compaction = {'class': 'TimeWindowCompactionStrategy'}
AND default_time_to_live = 7776000; -- 90 days
CREATE TABLE segment_speed_history (
segment_id bigint,
day_of_week smallint, -- 0-6
time_bucket smallint, -- 15-minute bucket, 0-95
p50_speed float,
p85_speed float,
sample_count int,
PRIMARY KEY (segment_id, day_of_week, time_bucket)
100M segments x 7 days x 96 buckets is ~67 billion rows at ~30 bytes = about 2 TB
TOTAL, not per day. THIS IS THE ACTUAL PRODUCT OF THE LOCATION PIPELINE, and
everything upstream is scaffolding.
Why Cassandra: 694,000 appends/sec with essentially no interactive reads - the most write-skewed workload in the system. LSM
storage makes every write a sequential memtable append, where a relational store would spend its life on random page updates
and index maintenance for rows nobody queries. And (user_id, bucket) rather than user_id alone because an active user
contributes ~17,000 samples/day and millions per year: a Cassandra partition is the unit of storage AND of repair, so
unbounded growth is an operational problem long before it is a storage one.
float is CORRECT here, unlike money. A float32 resolves latitude to ~1 metre, well below consumer GPS accuracy (3-10 m in the
open, far worse among buildings) - the MEASUREMENT error dwarfs the representation error, so precision loss is unobservable.
Money has no measurement error, which is what makes representation error the only error there is.
And default_time_to_live = 7776000 is a DESIGN POSITION, not a default. What the product actually needs is aggregate speed per
segment per time-of-day - a tiny derived table - so the raw traces expire and the aggregates persist. TWCS makes that expiry
drop whole SSTables rather than rewriting them: delete a file, not a row. Two reasons the aggregate is essential rather than
nice-to-have: a route requested for 8am TOMORROW has no live traffic to consult, and it is the fallback whenever a live
segment's TTL has expired - the common case for minor roads with few sampled vehicles. p85_speed sits alongside p50 because
for an ETA people rely on, the pessimistic percentile is often the more useful number: an estimate that is right half the time
is worse than one that is conservative.
Two directions of one product feature, two entirely unrelated index structures
FORWARD '1600 Amphitheatre Parkway, Mountain View, CA'
-> tokenize, normalize ('Pkwy'->'Parkway', case, accents)
-> inverted index lookup + fuzzy matching for typos
-> candidates ranked by prominence + query proximity
-> (lat, lng), place_id, precision level
REVERSE given a point, find the nearest addressable feature
-> an R-TREE or S2 CELL INDEX over address points and
street geometry
a spatial query, not a text one
Why a text-search engine and not a relational table: the query is fuzzy, multilingual, abbreviation-tolerant and typo-tolerant,
and WHERE address = ? answers approximately none of the queries people actually type. Conflating the two directions is a common
design error - they share a product feature and nothing else.
precision level is returned because it is honest AND actionable: ROOFTOP means the exact building, while RANGE_INTERPOLATED
means interpolated along a street segment and possibly tens of metres off. A navigation client should route to the STREET for
the latter rather than pretending to a precision it does not have. Results are heavily cached, since the same addresses are
searched repeatedly and a plain LRU absorbs most traffic.
Nothing in this system requires strong consistency anywhere - and that is the deep reason multi-region is easy
map tiles immutable per version; eventually consistent across edges a client is always on exactly ONE coherent
version, so there is no torn state. Version lag
just means some clients are on v41 and some on
v42 - both correct.
routing tiles immutable per version a route is computed entirely within one
version, so it cannot mix graphs
live traffic speeds eventual, seconds; last-write-wins an aggregate over a time window, so two
aggregators produce the same value - which is
why no leader election is needed
location history eventual, at-least-once a duplicate row with the same key is an
idempotent overwrite, so DUPLICATION IS
HARMLESS BY CONSTRUCTION and exactly-once
would be wasted effort
traffic aggregates eventual, batch a slightly stale historical average is
indistinguishable from a current one
route responses a READ-ONLY SNAPSHOT weights are read once at the start, so the
route is internally consistent even if the
world moved during computation
Every datum is either IMMUTABLE (tiles), STATISTICAL (traffic) or SELF-CORRECTING (positions). There is no global invariant to
protect - which is exactly why multi-region is easy here and the hardest unsolved problem in the digital wallet. And the
traffic aggregate has a genuinely pleasant scaling property: its row count is segments x days x buckets, so it does not grow
with usage at all.
What you'd revisit
segment_speed_history has a feedback loop nobody has modelled
it is trained on observed speeds, and those speeds were shaped by past routing decisions - so the model partly predicts its
own behaviour. Routing everyone around congestion creates congestion on the alternative, which the next aggregation observes
as newly slow. Real deployments split traffic across alternatives to damp this; that mechanism is absent from this schema.
the 90-day TTL is a policy assertion with no enforcement beyond Cassandra
a deletion request must also reach the Kafka backlog, the analytics warehouse and any object-storage archive. Cassandra
deletes are tombstones that reclaim no space until compaction, so 'deleted' and 'gone' differ by a compaction cycle.
turn restrictions and road attributes are underspecified
real routing needs time-of-day restrictions, vehicle-class restrictions (weight, height, hazmat), seasonal closures and bus
lanes. Each expands the edge record, and some make edge weights CONDITIONAL ON THE QUERY - which complicates the hierarchy's
assumption that a coarse tile's weights are usable by any route.
tile versioning assumes ONE GLOBAL version
a road change in Tokyo should not require republishing a version that Brazil then re-warms. Per-region versioning is probably
right, and it breaks the single tidy version endpoint.
no place / POI data at all
businesses, opening hours, reviews and photos are a large relational-plus-search dataset a real Maps product needs. The seam
(a place_id returned by geocoding that the proximity service resolves) is asserted rather than designed.
